advisor.summary: A nonqualified deferred compensation plan lets an owner-executive elect, before the service year, to take compensation later — moving income out of peak-rate years without qualified-plan dollar caps. Section 409A supplies the discipline: elections generally lock before the service year begins, payout timing is fixed up front against a short list of permissible events, and a failure triggers immediate inclusion, a 20% additional tax, and premium interest. Run the structural screen first, though: §404(a)(5) holds the employer's deduction until the year the executive includes the income, so a pass-through owner deferring against their own K-1 is usually just deferring their own deduction. The clean fact patterns are C-corporation owner-executives and sellers taking deferred comp or consulting payments from an unrelated buyer. Advisory by design — the value rides on future-rate assumptions the deterministic engine does not project.
mechanics: Election timing under §409A(a)(4): the deferral election must generally lock before January 1 of the service year; performance-based compensation gets a narrow exception running to six months before the period ends.

Distributions under §409A(a)(2) may occur only on six permissible events — separation from service, death, disability, a fixed date or schedule, change in control, or unforeseeable emergency — with no accelerations and no haircut withdrawals.

The arrangement must stay unfunded and unsecured: constructive receipt under Reg. §1.451-2 and the economic benefit doctrine tax any amount placed beyond the reach of general creditors — which is why a rabbi trust works and a secured account does not.
The employer's deduction waits under §404(a)(5) until the executive's inclusion year — the matching rule that makes routine pass-through owner deferrals self-defeating.

FICA follows the special timing rule of §3121(v)(2): deferred amounts are FICA-taxed at vesting rather than at payment — often cheap for an executive already past the wage base, with the eventual payout then FICA-free.

authority.note: The governing statute for every NQDC arrangement — election timing, the six distribution events, anti-acceleration, and the inclusion-plus-20%-plus-interest cost of failure.
The regulations' definitional core — deferral of compensation, separation from service, specified employees, and plan aggregation all live here.
Holds the employer's deduction until the inclusion year — the provision that screens out most pass-through owner deferrals.
Constructive receipt — compensation credited, set apart, or made available without substantial limitation is taxed now; every plan design must clear it.
The FICA special timing rule — deferred comp is FICA-taxed at vesting, often an advantage above the Social Security wage base.

requirements: A written plan that satisfies §409A in both form and operation before the first deferral election is signed.
The right taxpayer profile: a C-corporation owner-executive, a key employee, or a seller deferring payments from an unrelated buyer — not an S-corp owner deferring against their own K-1.
Elections signed and documented before the service year, with the payout schedule fixed in the election itself.
Employer credit quality the executive can accept — deferred amounts are an unsecured claim, and a rabbi trust cures change-of-heart risk, never insolvency risk.
risks: The leading exposure is a §409A operational failure — an early payment, a discretionary acceleration, a late election — triggering immediate inclusion of all vested deferrals plus the 20% additional tax and premium interest; the penalty routinely dwarfs the benefit sought.
Credit risk is structural: participants stand as general unsecured creditors, and an employer bankruptcy can erase decades of deferrals with no offsetting tax relief.
Deferring at known rates into unknown ones is a wager — legislation or a spike year at payout can invert the arbitrage entirely.
For pass-through owners, §404(a)(5) usually reduces the play to a wash or worse; run the combined owner-plus-entity math before claiming any benefit.

State trailing tax: deferred comp earned in one state can remain taxable there after a move unless paid as substantially equal periodic payments over ten years or more under the federal pension-sourcing statute (4 U.S.C. §114).
stateNotes: Missouri conforms to the federal inclusion timing through its federal-AGI starting point (RSMo §143.121) — deferred amounts reach the Missouri return in the same year they reach the federal one.
The PTET interaction is timing-only: federal law defers the entity's deduction to the inclusion year, so a Missouri pass-through entity tax election (RSMo §143.436) sees no base reduction until then.

Missouri-specific: compensation earned in Missouri and paid to a retiree who has left the state can remain Missouri-source unless structured as periodic payments over ten years or more — design the payout with a possible move in mind.
reviewChecklist: Fact-pattern screen documented in the file: entity type, expected rate path at payout, and employer credit quality all support deferral.
Plan documents drafted or reviewed by executive-comp counsel and tested against §409A in both form and operation.
Deferral elections dated before the service year, with payout events and schedules fixed in the election itself.
Rabbi trust or other security measures weighed, with the executive's unsecured-creditor status acknowledged in writing.
Annual operations audit calendared — payments exactly on schedule, no accelerations, W-2 reporting correct.

client.teaser: Pick the year — and the tax rate — your biggest paydays land in.
client.headline: Earn it now, collect it later — in a lower-tax year
plainEnglish: You normally pay tax on pay in the year you earn it, even if that is your highest-rate year ever. A deferred compensation plan is a formal agreement, made ahead of time, to receive part of your pay in a later year. You pay tax when the money arrives, ideally at a much lower rate.

The rules are strict. You must choose to defer before you earn the money. The payout schedule locks in from day one. Breaking the rules brings steep penalties. So the plan comes with real legal paperwork, done once and done right.

One honest caveat. For most S corporation and partnership owners, deferring your own pay also defers your own deduction, and the math cancels out. This plan shines for C corporation owners and for owners selling to an outside buyer.
client.analogy: Think of a dam on a river of income. Instead of the whole flow landing in flood years, you release it in the years where it does the least damage.
benefits: Shifts income from peak-rate years into lower-rate years
No dollar caps like a 401(k) — you can defer large amounts
Can be built around retirement or the sale of your business
Doubles as a retention tool for key employees
steps: WE screen whether your entity and plans truly benefit — and tell you plainly if they do not.
WE bring in a specialist attorney to draft the plan documents.
YOU sign your deferral election before each year begins; the payout schedule locks then.
WE audit the plan each year so the strict rules stay satisfied.
clientCommitments: Sign deferral elections before the year starts — a late election cannot be fixed
Accept that deferred money is an unsecured promise from the company until it is paid
Never ask for an early or changed payout — the rules do not allow one

annualMaintenance: Calendar and sign deferral elections before each service year
Annual §409A operations audit — payments exactly on schedule, no accelerations
Review employer credit quality and rabbi-trust funding; confirm W-2 Box 11 reporting at distributions
